english: I'd like to send a parcel
usage: I'd like to send a parcel
Polite; your opening line at the post office or parcel counter
반말, to a friend or a familiar convenience-store clerk
I'd like to send a parcel, please
Softer, fuller form with 좀 and the trailing -는데요
I'd like to send this off
부치다 ('to send/post') instead of 보내다, slightly more 'post office' flavored
examples: 택배 보내려고요.
I'd like to send a parcel.
Said as you set the box on the counter; the staff takes it from there
이거 택배로 보내려고요. 얼마예요?
I want to send this by parcel. How much is it?
택배로 ('by parcel') marks the method, then ask the price
부산까지 택배 보내려고 하는데요, 오늘 보내면 언제 도착해요?
I'd like to send a parcel to Busan — if I send it today, when does it arrive?
까지 ('to/as far as') marks the destination city
nuance: 택배 보내려고요 is 택배 ('courier parcel', Sino-Korean 宅配, lit. 'home-delivery') + 보내다 ('to send') in the -려고요 form, which states YOUR intention: 'I intend to send a parcel.' That -려고(요) ending is the natural, soft way to announce why you've walked up to a counter — it signals a plan and gently invites the staff to help, rather than barking an order. 택배 specifically means a courier package delivered to a door (by 우체국택배, CJ대한통운, etc.), as opposed to 우편/편지 (ordinary mail/letters) — so use 택배 for boxes and goods, not for a simple letter. The near-synonym verb 부치다 ('to post/send off') is interchangeable here (택배 부치려고요) and sounds a touch more classic-post-office; 보내다 is the everyday default. The English-speaker pitfall is over-translating 'I want to send' as 보내고 싶어요 ('I desire to send'), which sounds like confessing a wish rather than doing a transaction; Koreans announce the action with -려고요. Another trap is saying 택배 하려고요 ('I want to do parcel') — 하다 doesn't fit; the verb is 보내다 or 부치다. Default to 보내려고요 with staff; with a friend drop to 보내려고.

english: Please send this by registered mail
usage: Please send this by registered mail
Polite; the standard request for tracked, signed-for mail
반말, to a friend handling it for you
Could you send it by registered mail?
Short version once you've already handed over the item
examples: 이거 등기로 보내 주세요.
Please send this by registered mail.
Said for important documents you want tracked and signed for
계약서라서 등기로 보내 주세요. 안전하게요.
It's a contract, so please send it registered — safely.
Give the reason (계약서, 'a contract') so they understand why you want 등기
일반우편이랑 등기랑 가격 차이 얼마나 나요? 등기로 보내 주세요.
How much is the difference between regular and registered? Send it registered.
Compare 일반우편 vs 등기 before choosing
nuance: 이거 등기로 보내 주세요 is 이거 ('this') + 등기 ('registered mail', Sino-Korean 登記, lit. 'registration') + -로 ('by/via', the method particle) + 보내 주세요 ('please send for me'). 등기(우편) is mail that is logged, tracked, and requires the recipient's signature on delivery — you use it for contracts, official documents, anything you must prove arrived. The crucial particle is -로, which marks the METHOD ('by registered'); leaving it out (등기 보내 주세요) sounds off, and using the wrong particle (등기를) makes 등기 the object rather than the manner. The sharp contrast is 등기 vs 일반우편 ('ordinary mail'): 일반우편 is cheap, untracked, no signature — fine for a postcard but risky for documents; 등기 costs more but is provable. Don't confuse 등기 (registered MAIL) with 등기부등본 (a property-registration certificate) — same 등기 root, totally different errand. The English-speaker pitfall is calling it 'certified mail' and trying to coin 인증우편, which isn't the term; the real word is 등기. Also, learners often forget the favor verb and say 등기로 보내요, which describes rather than requests — keep 보내 주세요 to actually ask the clerk to do it. Default 존댓말; with a friend, 등기로 보내 줘.

english: Could you tell me the tracking number?
usage: Could you tell me the tracking number?
Polite; asking the clerk for the number to track the parcel
반말, asking a friend who sent it
운송장 = the fuller word; 어떻게 돼요 is the natural 'what is it'
Please text me the tracking number
문자로 ('by text') to get it sent to your phone
examples: 송장 번호 좀 알려 주세요.
Could you tell me the tracking number?
Asked right after you hand over the parcel and pay
택배 보냈는데 송장 번호로 조회하면 돼요?
I sent a parcel — can I track it with the tracking number?
조회하다 ('to look up') is the verb for checking a parcel's status
송장 번호 받았는데 아직 조회가 안 돼요. 언제부터 떠요?
I got the tracking number but it's not showing yet. When does it appear?
뜨다 ('to come up / show on screen') is how Koreans say tracking 'appears'
nuance: 송장 번호 좀 알려 주세요 is 송장 ('waybill/invoice slip', Sino-Korean 送狀, the shipping label on a parcel) + 번호 ('number') + 좀 (softener) + 알려 주세요 ('please let me know'). The 송장 is the slip stuck on the box; its 송장 번호 (also called 운송장 번호 or 택배 번호) is what you punch into a tracking site to follow the parcel. The verb you pair with it is 조회하다 ('to look up/track'), and on screen Koreans say the info 뜨다/뜨다 ('comes up'). A key distinction: 송장 ('shipping waybill') is NOT 영수증 ('the receipt') — the 송장 number tracks the parcel, the 영수증 proves you paid; asking for the wrong one gets you the wrong slip. Note 송장 also means a commercial 'invoice' in trade contexts, but at a parcel counter it's the shipping label. The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'tracking number' literally as 추적 번호 — understandable, and 추적 ('tracking') exists, but the everyday term Koreans actually use is 송장 번호 / 운송장 번호. Another slip is using 가르치다 ('to teach') instead of 알려 주다 ('to inform'): 송장 번호 가르쳐 주세요 sounds like asking for a lesson; 알려 주세요 is 'let me know.' Default 존댓말; with a friend, 알려 줘.

Using 가르쳐 주세요 instead of 알려 주세요.
가르치다 means 'to teach (a skill)'. To ask someone to tell you a number, use 알려 주다: 송장 번호 좀 알려 주세요.

usage: Polite; the receiver pays the shipping fee on delivery
Short form once the parcel is already on the counter
Please send it prepaid (I pay now)
The opposite: 선불, sender pays up front — useful to contrast
examples: 착불로 보내 주세요.
Please send it cash-on-delivery.
Said when the person receiving it will pay the shipping
받는 분이 낼 거예요. 착불로 보내 주세요.
The recipient will pay — send it C.O.D.
받는 분 ('the recipient') makes clear who pays
선불이에요, 착불이에요? — 착불로 보내 주세요. 상대방이 내기로 했어요.
Is it prepaid or C.O.D.? — C.O.D., please. The other person agreed to pay.
Answering the clerk's 선불/착불 question; 상대방 = 'the other party'
nuance: 착불로 보내 주세요 is 착불 ('payment on arrival', Sino-Korean 着拂, lit. 'pay-on-arrival') + -로 ('by', method particle) + 보내 주세요 ('please send'). 착불 means the RECIPIENT pays the shipping fee when the parcel is handed to them — extremely common in Korea for online resale (중고거래), returns, and favors. Its exact opposite is 선불 ('prepay', 先拂), where the SENDER pays at the counter now. The clerk will often ask 선불이에요, 착불이에요?, and this is your answer — so getting the pair straight is essential: 착불 = receiver pays later, 선불 = sender pays now. The method particle -로 is required (착불로); 착불을 would wrongly make it the object. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 착불 to 'C.O.D.' and assuming it means the receiver pays for the GOODS — no, in Korean parcels 착불 almost always refers only to the SHIPPING FEE, not the product price. Another trap is courteously deciding 착불 for someone without telling them — socially you should confirm the recipient agreed, since they'll be charged at their door. Don't confuse 착불 with 반품 ('return of goods'); they often co-occur (returns are frequently sent 착불) but mean different things. Default 존댓말; with a friend, 착불로 보내 줘.

english: It's fragile, so please handle it carefully
usage: It's fragile, so please handle it carefully
Polite; warning staff the contents can break
It's breakable, so handle it carefully
반말, to a friend or mover
파손 주의 스티커 좀 붙여 주세요
Please put a 'Fragile' sticker on it
파손 주의 = the printed 'handle with care' label
There's glass inside. It breaks easily
Stating the risk plainly; 깨지기 쉽다 = 'easy to break'
examples: 깨지는 거라서 조심히 다뤄 주세요.
It's fragile, so please handle it carefully.
Said as you hand over a box with breakables
안에 그릇이 있어서요, 파손 주의로 보내 주세요.
There are dishes inside, so please send it as 'fragile'.
파손 주의로 marks the fragile-handling option you want
이거 깨지기 쉬운 거예요. 위에 뭐 올리지 말아 주세요.
This breaks easily. Please don't stack anything on top.
위에 ('on top') + 올리다 ('to place on') for a stacking warning
nuance: 깨지는 거라서 조심히 다뤄 주세요 is 깨지는 거 (깨지다 'to break/shatter' + 거 'thing' = 'a breakable thing') + -라서 ('because it is') + 조심히 ('carefully') + 다뤄 주세요 (다루다 'to handle' + 주세요 = 'please handle for me'). It warns staff or a mover that the contents are fragile. The verb pairing matters: 깨지다 is INTRANSITIVE ('it breaks/shatters on its own'), which is why you describe the object as 깨지는 거 — learners wrongly reach for 깨다 ('to break something deliberately'), but you're not smashing it, so 깨지다 is correct. The post-office set term is 파손 주의 ('caution: breakage', the printed Fragile label), so a very natural request is 파손 주의로 보내 주세요 or asking for the 파손 주의 스티커. Contrast 조심히 다뤄 주세요 ('handle carefully', a general plea) with 파손 주의로 해 주세요 (asking for the official fragile-handling/label) — the second is the concrete service. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 'be careful' → 조심하세요, which tells the PERSON to be careful (almost like a warning to watch themselves) rather than asking them to handle the BOX gently; 조심히 다뤄 주세요 keeps the focus on the parcel. Also avoid 부서지다 confusion: 부서지다 is for things crumbling/falling apart (furniture), while glass and ceramics 깨지다. Default 존댓말; with a friend, 조심히 다뤄 줘.

english: Can I buy a box here?
usage: Can I buy a box here?
Polite-neutral; asking if packing boxes are for sale
파나요 ('do you sell') is the most natural shop phrasing
포장 박스 = a packing/shipping box; 있어요 asks if they have it
examples: 박스 하나 살 수 있어요?
Can I buy a box?
Asked when you arrived without packaging
여기 박스도 팔아요? 제일 작은 거로 하나 주세요.
Do you sell boxes too? Give me one of the smallest.
제일 작은 거로 ('the smallest one') picks a size
짐이 좀 큰데, 큰 박스 있어요? 테이프도 같이 주세요.
My stuff's a bit big — do you have a large box? Give me tape too.
Add 테이프 ('tape') to pack it on the spot
nuance: 박스 하나 살 수 있어요? is 박스 (loanword 'box') + 하나 ('one') + 살 수 있어요? (살다→사다 'to buy' + -ㄹ 수 있다 'can/be able' = 'can I buy?'). Post offices and convenience stores sell 우체국 택배 박스 in numbered sizes (1호, 2호, 3호…), so this is a practical first step when you show up with loose items. The natural shop alternative is 박스 파나요? ('do you sell boxes?') or 박스 있어요? ('do you have boxes?') — Koreans very often ask availability with 있어요/파나요 rather than the literal 'can I buy.' A subtle distinction: 박스 (box) is the loanword everyone uses for a shipping carton, while 상자 is the native word — both are fine, but 박스 is more colloquial for parcels. Stack concrete steps: 완충재 + 테이프, ending with 안 터지게요
nuance: 박스 안 터지게 단단히 포장해 주세요 is 박스 ('box') + 안 ('not') + 터지게 (터지다 'to burst/split open' + -게 'so that') + 단단히 ('firmly/sturdily') + 포장해 주세요 (포장하다 'to pack/wrap', Sino-Korean 包裝 + 주세요). The -게 of 터지게 means 'so that/in such a way' and, with 안, expresses purpose-of-prevention: 'so that it does NOT burst.' This 안 ...-게 (해 주세요) frame is the natural way to request an outcome you want to AVOID. 단단히 ('firmly, solidly') is the adverb of choice for secure packing (from 단단하다 'to be hard/firm'); a near-synonym is 꼼꼼히 ('thoroughly/meticulously'), which stresses care/detail rather than tightness — use 단단히 for strength, 꼼꼼히 for thoroughness. The verb 터지다 is intransitive ('it bursts open by itself'), correct for a box giving way; don't use 깨지다 (that's for fragile contents shattering) — the BOX 터지다, the GLASS inside 깨지다. The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 'pack it well' → 잘 포장해 주세요, which is fine but vague; specifying 단단히/안 터지게 communicates exactly what 'well' means and is more effective with staff. Another slip is placing the negative wrong: 박스 터지게 안 포장해 주세요 muddles it — keep 안 on the bursting: 안 터지게. Concrete add-ons: 완충재/뽁뽁이 (cushioning/bubble wrap) and 테이프 (tape). Default 존댓말; with a friend, 단단히 포장해 줘.

깨지다 is for fragile things shattering (glass); a box gives way with 터지다. So 'so the box won't burst' is 박스 안 터지게.

hangul: 택배가 안 왔는데 어떻게 된 거예요?
english: My parcel hasn't come — what's going on?
usage: 택배가 안 왔는데 어떻게 된 거예요?
My parcel hasn't come — what's going on?
Polite; querying a missing or delayed delivery
택배가 안 왔는데 어떻게 된 거야?
My parcel hasn't come — what's up?
반말, to a friend or familiar courier
Tracking says delivered but I didn't get it
Reporting a mismatch between tracking and reality
분실된 것 같은데 확인 좀 해 주세요
I think it's lost — could you check?
분실되다 ('to be lost') for a missing parcel
examples: 택배가 안 왔는데 어떻게 된 거예요?
My parcel hasn't come — what's going on?
Calling the carrier when a parcel is overdue
3일 전에 보냈다는데 아직도 안 왔어요. 어떻게 된 거예요?
They say it was sent 3 days ago but it still hasn't come. What's going on?
Give the timeline (3일 전) to push for an answer
송장에는 배송 완료라는데 저는 못 받았어요. 분실된 거 아니에요? 확인 좀 부탁드려요.
The waybill says delivered, but I didn't get it. Isn't it lost? Please check.
배송 완료 ('delivery complete') vs reality; 부탁드려요 to request firmly but politely
nuance: 택배가 안 왔는데 어떻게 된 거예요? is 택배 ('parcel') + 가 (subject) + 안 왔는데 (안 'not' + 오다 'come', past 왔다 + -는데 soft connective) + 어떻게 ('how') + 된 거예요? (되다 'to become/turn out' + -ㄴ 거예요 = 'what has it become / what's the situation?'). The set phrase 어떻게 된 거예요? literally 'how did it become?' is the standard way to ask 'what's going on / what happened?' about a problem — firm but not rude, leaning on the impersonal 되다 ('turn out') rather than blaming a person. The -는데 again links your situation ('it hasn't come, so…') to the question, softening the complaint. Useful companion vocabulary: 배송 조회 ('tracking lookup'), 배송 완료 ('delivery complete' status), 분실 ('loss/missing', 紛失), 지연 ('delay', 遲延). A key contrast: 어떻게 된 거예요? asks for an explanation of the situation, whereas 어떡해요? (어떻게 해요?) means 'what do I do / what now?' — don't swap them; the first seeks info, the second seeks a remedy. The English-speaker pitfall is the angry-sounding 직역 'why didn't it come?' → 왜 안 왔어요?, which can read as accusatory toward the listener; the neutral 어떻게 된 거예요? (or adding 혹시, 'by any chance') keeps it civil while still pressing for answers. Also note 오다's subject is the parcel (택배가 안 왔다), not you. Default 존댓말; with a friend, 어떻게 된 거야?.
